There is a particular kind of silence that doesn't live in empty rooms.

It lives in full ones. It lives in the public library on a Tuesday at 3:47 PM when the rain has been falling since morning and the old radiators are hissing and everyone inside has given up on being anywhere else. The silence there isn't the absence of sound. It's the accumulation of it. Pages turning, someone coughing, a chair scraping, the soft thump of a book bag dropped to the floor. All those tiny sounds layer on top of each other until they invert and become a kind of hush. A thick, inhabited quiet.

I used to go there not to read but to watch people read. I had a job that required me to be online twelve hours a day, and I had started to develop a superstition that my thoughts were not my own anymore, that they had been pre-chewed by whatever feed I had looked at last. So I would go to the library to remember what an unmediated thought felt like.

One afternoon, I noticed an old woman who came in at almost exactly the same time I did. She always sat at the same long oak table near the reference section, table six. She never brought a book with her. She would go to the stacks, pull three or four enormous books — art books, atlases, bound volumes of old Life magazines — and she would just sit and look at them. Not read. Look. For an hour she would slowly turn pages, her finger sometimes hovering an inch above a photograph. Her face never changed much. It was a face that had decided, a long time ago, that it didn't need to perform reactions for anyone.

I became obsessed with what she was doing. Because it seemed to me that she was practicing a lost art. We know how to skim, how to search, how to extract information. We have forgotten how to simply look at something without needing it to become useful.

We are taught, from a very young age, that attention is a resource to be spent wisely. Pay attention. Don't pay attention to that. Attention is currency. But no one teaches us that attention is also a lens, and that what you see depends entirely on the shape of the lens you are looking through, and that most of us never clean the lens at all.

For example — light. We talk about light as if it's one thing. But the light at 7 AM in June is a completely different substance than the light at 4 PM in November. The June light is declarative. It says, "I am here, everything is possible, go outside." The November light is interrogative. It comes in low and sideways through the window, it makes dust visible, and it asks, "Are you sure? Are you sure about what you're doing?" And yet we have one word for it.

The old woman in the library understood this. I realized it the third time I watched her. She wasn't looking at pictures of the Grand Canyon or the surface of the moon. She was looking at the way the light fell in those pictures. She was collecting light.

I started to do the same thing without meaning to. I would leave the library and I would be unable to go back to staring at my phone immediately, so my eyes had to land somewhere. On the wet asphalt. On the way the neon sign from the Chinese restaurant across the street was reflected and broken into a hundred trembling orange pieces in the puddles. On the back of a man's coat where the rain had made a dark continent.

One day, and this sounds made up but it isn't, I swear it isn't, a pigeon landed on the windowsill next to table six. City pigeons are usually frantic, neurotic creatures, bobbing and twitching. This one was still. It was wet. It had that deep, iridescent grey-purple on its neck, and it was looking inside. The old woman looked up from her atlas, looked at the pigeon, and the pigeon looked at her. And for about ten seconds, there was absolutely no barrier between them. Not a cute Disney moment. Not anthropomorphism. Just two living things acknowledging each other in a room full of paper.

Then the librarian coughed and the pigeon left.

That night I went home and I couldn't sleep because I kept thinking about the pigeon and about attention and about what it means to see something as it actually is, not as a symbol for something else. A pigeon is almost always a symbol. In a city, it means dirt, or persistence, or rats with wings, or if you're feeling poetic, it means home. But that afternoon, for ten seconds, it wasn't a symbol. It was just a pigeon.

We have built an entire civilization on symbolism. That's what language is, after all. A symbol system so advanced that we forget it is a system at all. You say the word "chair" and I see a chair, but there is no chair here. We are hallucinating together, politely. Money is a symbol. Borders are symbols. Time, as we measure it — 3:47 PM — is a symbol laid on top of something that does not, in itself, have numbers. The real world is continuous. Our symbols are discrete. So there will always be a gap. And in that gap lives all of our anxiety.

Because what do you do when you realize you have been living in the map and not the territory? You can't just burn the map. You need the map to get to work.

This is where I think we get stuck. We think we have to choose. Either be a practical person who lives in symbols, who pays rent and shows up to meetings on time, or be some kind of enlightened dropout who sits on a mountain and watches pigeons. But the old woman was neither. She was in the middle. She used the library — perhaps the most symbolic institution we have, a building full of maps — to practice contact with the territory.

I think that is what art is actually for. Not decoration. Not status. Not even self-expression, exactly. I think art is the training ground for that kind of contact.

When you stand in front of a Rothko painting and your eyes start to hurt because there is nothing to "get," you are being asked to stop extracting and start seeing. When you listen to a piece of music that doesn't have lyrics, that doesn't tell you what to feel, you are being asked to feel something that hasn't been pre-labeled. When you read a novel that doesn't have a tidy moral, you are being asked to hold more than one contradictory idea without immediately resolving it.

And this is difficult work. It's much harder than solving a problem.

Our brains are problem-solving engines. Give it a problem — how do I get food, how do I answer this email, how do I fix this relationship — and it lights up. Give it something that is not a problem, something that is just there, like the light on a wet street or a pigeon on a sill, and it doesn't know what to do. It gets itchy. It wants to turn the pigeon into a to-do list item: "Look up why pigeons are iridescent." "Remember to buy birdseed." It wants to turn the light into a photograph to post.

To not do that takes a kind of muscle that we are not taught to exercise.

I started to practice. Small exercises. When I was waiting for the kettle to boil, instead of checking my phone, I would watch the tiny bubbles form on the bottom of the metal before they rose. When I was on the bus, I would look at one person's hands and try to imagine their whole life from the shape of their knuckles, but then I would stop myself and just look at the hands themselves — the cracks, the veins, the small scar.

It's embarrassing how bad I was at it at first. My attention span was like a terrified hamster. Ten seconds, then dart away.

But slowly, like any muscle, it got stronger.

And the world got bigger.

This is the paradox that no one tells you: when you pay close, non-extractive attention to small things, the world doesn't get smaller and more detailed, it gets larger and more mysterious. That puddle that reflects the neon sign is not just a puddle. It contains optics, and weather, and electricity, and migration — because that neon sign was made somewhere, and the gas inside it came from somewhere, and the rain came from an ocean — and all of it is right there, in a six-inch circle of water on cracked asphalt. If you really look, you fall through it.

I began to understand why children are so tired all the time. They are falling through every puddle.

We tell ourselves that we grow up and become more sophisticated. In some ways we do. But in another, very real way, we grow up and become more filtered. We learn to ignore 99.9% of what is there so that we can function. The price of functioning is a kind of blindness. It's a necessary blindness, but we forget we are wearing the blinders. We start to think the tunnel is the whole sky.

A few weeks after the pigeon incident, the old woman didn't come. Table six was empty. I felt a stupid, outsized sense of loss, as if a landmark had been removed. I went to the stacks and tried to do what she did. I pulled down a massive book of Ansel Adams photographs. I sat where she sat and I looked. I tried to look at light.

After about twenty minutes, the librarian, a young man with a tattoo of a small anchor behind his ear, came over and said, as gently as possible, that the library would be closing in fifteen minutes.

I nodded. As I was putting the books back, a small, folded piece of paper fell out of one of them. It was not old, not a lost 1950s checkout slip. It was printer paper, folded twice. Inside, in neat, blue ballpoint, in handwriting that I recognized even though I had never seen it before, was written:

"Things don't become interesting. You become interested. - A."

A.

Her initial. I looked around. The library was almost empty.

I kept the note. I still have it taped to my refrigerator, though the ink has faded a little.

I never saw her again. I don't know if A. stands for Anne, or Alice, or Ahmed. I don't know if she moved, or got sick, or just found a different library. But she left me that sentence, and that sentence turned out to be an entire operating system.

Things don't become interesting. You become interested.

It means interest is not a property of objects; it is a capacity of the subject. It is a verb, not an adjective. The world is not divided into interesting and boring things. It is divided into people who have practiced interest and people who have not.

And if that's true, then boredom is not a problem with the world. It's a problem with my attention. Which is actually incredibly good news. Because I cannot control the world. I cannot make world events more interesting, I cannot make my job consistently interesting, I cannot make traffic interesting. But I can, to some degree, train my capacity to be interested.

This is not the same as positive thinking. It's not "look on the bright side." It's not pretending that something dull is exciting. It's a quieter, more honest thing. It's saying: "There is more here than I am currently perceiving, and I will look a little longer."

I think about that sentence when I read about science. People imagine that scientists are interested because the universe is interesting. It's the other way around. The universe was here being exactly as interesting as it is now when everyone thought it was made of four elements and moved by angels. It's not more interesting now because we have electron microscopes. We are just more interested, and so more of its interest has become visible to us. Interest is the telescope, not the star.

I think about that sentence when I hear people talk about love. We talk about finding an interesting person. But long-term love is not about finding an interesting person and coasting. It's about the practice of remaining interested in a person who you think you have already fully mapped. Any person, looked at closely enough, is bottomless. But you have to keep looking.

The other day I walked home a different way. Not because I was trying to be mindful or spontaneous or any of those words that have been turned into hashtags. But because the main street was blocked for construction. So I turned down a side street I had never been down, even though I had lived in this neighborhood for three years.

It was a street of small, identical houses, but one house had filled its entire front yard with wooden sculptures that moved in the wind. Not wind chimes. Sculptures — figures made of scrap wood, painted bright colors, with arms that waved, with propellers. There were at least twenty of them. A man in his seventies was out front adjusting one of them with a wrench.

I stopped. He looked up and said, "They're too loud when the wind is high, but I like them loud."

I said they were wonderful.

He said, "My wife says it's junk. I say it's company."

And we both laughed.

If I had not been forced to take that detour, I would never have seen it. But also, if I had not been practicing, in my tiny, hamster-attention way, the art of looking, I would have walked right past it while looking at my phone. The detour gave me the opportunity. The practice let me take it.

I am not a mystical person. I don't believe the universe is sending me messages through wind sculptures. I believe in statistics and maintenance. But I do believe this: the world is constantly offering this kind of small, unrecorded exchange, and we miss most of it because we are skimming.

We skim because we are afraid. If we look too long, we might feel something. If we feel something, we might have to do something. It's safer to move.

But every once in a while, you look a little longer. You let the pigeon look back. You let the light be interrogative. You let the note in the book be from a stranger who will never know how much it meant.

And then, for a second, the map and the territory align. Not perfectly. Never perfectly. But enough that you can feel the ground again.

That is all I wanted to say. I started with silence in a library. I am ending here, in this room, wherever you are reading this. There is light falling somewhere near you right now. On the floor, on your hand, on the rim of a cup. It has traveled 93 million miles to get there, bounced off something, and landed. It's asking a question. You don't have to answer it. You can just notice it.

You can become interested.
